intro:
A BigCommerce store I work on needed full GA4 ecommerce tracking through Google Tag Manager, so I went looking for something ready-made. Google gave me guides and service pages. After a long search, the scripts I ended up with came from people sharing them on YouTube, one script per event.

They got events moving. Then I logged what was really being sent. The same $9.99 cable was reported as $10.69 when added to the cart, because tax had leaked into the price. Changing a quantity on the cart page sent nothing at all, and enhanced conversions only worked because two separate scripts happened to merge in GTM.

So I built the one script I had been looking for, tested it on that store through to a real paid order, and made it free. This is how it went, told in the order you'd do it yourself, with every step and screenshot you need. That includes the mistake that passes every test in Preview and still breaks live.
tldr: Turn on BigCommerce's data layer. Add the free tracker as one GTM Custom HTML tag or one Script Manager script, never both, or import the ready-made GTM container. Send its events to GA4 and Google Ads, map user_data to a User-Provided Data variable, remove every old ecommerce script, test in Preview, publish, confirm the published container really contains your changes, and finish with one real paid order.
sections: What I found when I searched

Before building anything, I looked again, properly this time. Here's what is out there today, so you can judge for yourself:

OptionWhat it isWhere it fell short for me
BigCommerce's native GA4 connectionBuilt in, under Data Solutions. Sends the standard ecommerce events from BigCommerce's own data layerIt doesn't go through your GTM setup, and you can't add custom parameters
fueled-io/bigcommerce-datalayerThe closest match: open source, GA4 format, installed through Script Manager, GPL-3 licensedIts last commit is from June 2022. It does not use BODL, and its README has no shipping step or enhanced conversions
Purchase-only guidesFor example this GTM guide and this one. Useful explanations of the purchase eventThey stop at the purchase, or describe the rest without a script to install
Scripts shared on YouTubeUsually one script per eventYou collect them yourself, and nothing checks that they agree with each other
Tag Manager SuiteA BigCommerce app, $4.99 a month when I checked. Installs and manages GTMIts listing doesn't mention GA4 or enhanced conversions
Agencies, such as scandiwebA paid, done-for-you implementationA good route if you have the budget, but not a script you can install

I couldn't find a free, maintained script covering the whole funnel with enhanced conversions data. That doesn't prove there isn't one, only that a long search didn't turn one up. So I decided to build it, and to start by finding out why simply connecting BigCommerce's data to GA4 wasn't enough.
Why not connect BODL straight to GA4?

With nothing ready to install, I looked at what BigCommerce itself provides. It has a data layer called BODL, the Big Open Data Layer, and the obvious shortcut is to connect it straight to GA4. Before writing any tracking, I logged what it actually sends on the live store. It's a good source of events, but this is what the log showed:

  • Tax in the price: AJAX add and remove payloads carried $10.69 in sale_price for a $9.99 item. The cart page payload said $9.99.
  • Stock counted as quantity: on product pages, quantity held stock on hand. That cable showed 198, so price times quantity would report $1,978.02 for one product view.
  • Missing quantity changes: raising a quantity from 1 to 2 on the cart page fired no add event.
  • Repeat checkout events: add_payment_info fired on reaching the payment step and again after a coupon was applied.
  • No purchase event to rely on: bodl_v1_order_purchased did not fire on my $0 test order, so purchase reads the Orders API instead.

The script keeps BODL as the trigger and takes prices from the Cart and Orders APIs. It also compares the cart before and after each change to catch what BODL misses.
What the script tracks

The log gave me a clear brief: keep BODL as the trigger, take prices from the APIs, and push one clean funnel from a single script. This is what came out of it.

EventWhen it firesWhere the data comes from
view_item_listCategory or brand pageBODL
select_itemClick on a product card in that listBODL and the page
view_itemProduct pageBODL
searchKeyword searchBODL
add_to_cartAdd, or quantity raised on the cart pageBODL and Cart API
remove_from_cartRemove, or quantity loweredBODL and Cart API
view_cartCart page, unless emptyCart API
begin_checkoutOnce per cartBODL and Cart API
add_shipping_infoOnce per cartBODL and Cart API
add_payment_infoOnce per cartBODL and Cart API
purchaseConfirmation page, once per orderOrders API
purchase_testSame, for a coupon you mark as a testOrders API

The script also pushes user_info with only a user ID for logged-in shoppers, and bc_ecom_error if BigCommerce stops looking the way the script expects.
Before you start

What follows is what I did on that store, in the order you should do it. You'll need:

  • A BigCommerce Stencil store. Headless and Catalyst stores don't have this checkout or BODL setup.
  • GTM installed on all pages, including checkout and order confirmation. Check by viewing those pages in Preview.
  • Publish access in GTM, and access to BigCommerce Settings and Script Manager.
  • A list of every ecommerce script already running, so you can remove them in Step 8.
Step 1: Turn on the BigCommerce data layer

My first step had nothing to do with GTM. The whole script depends on BODL, and BODL sits behind a setting that's hidden by default.

Go to Settings > Data solutions, scroll down, click Show advanced settings, and tick Turn on the data layer (Required for Google Analytics 4).

[[img:bc-data-layer-setting|The setting is hidden until you expand advanced settings.]]
Don't skip this. With it off, the script loads but no browsing or checkout events reach the dataLayer, and GTM Preview shows bc_ecom_error with bodl_missing. It's easy to miss because nothing in Script Manager or GTM points to it.
Step 2: Choose how to install it

With the data available, the next decision was where the script should live. I wanted both GTM and Script Manager available, so anyone could pick what suits their store. Each comes pasted or hosted, which makes four files.

Install one option only. All four push the same events, and a second copy on the same page does nothing.

OptionFileBest for
GTM, pastedgtm-paste.htmlMost stores. You get Preview, versions and rollback, and nothing changes unless you change it
GTM, hostedgtm-hosted.htmlSeveral stores that should all get 1.x fixes automatically
Script Manager, pastedscript-manager-paste.htmlContainers that block Custom HTML
Script Manager, hostedscript-manager-hosted.htmlThe same, with automatic 1.x fixes

I recommend GTM, pasted. Files are on GitHub, and the listener page has direct downloads.

Hosted files and PCI. BigCommerce asks for an integrity hash on URL-type scripts that run on checkout (PCI DSS 6.4.3). The hosted options load from a small inline script, so no hash is enforced, and a future 1.x update can change what runs on your checkout. If the store has PCI requirements, use a pasted file or pin an exact version such as @1.0.0, and add the script to your PCI inventory.
Neither option updates itself when BigCommerce changes. Someone still has to ship a fix. The health event in Step 10 is how you find out one is needed.
Step 3: Add the tag in GTM

For this store I chose GTM, because Preview, versions and rollback make a change like this much safer.

The fast route: import the ready-made container

Once this was working, I packaged the whole setup into one file, so you don't have to build Steps 3 to 7 by hand. Download the GTM import file, or get it from GitHub.

  1. In GTM, go to Admin > Import Container and choose the file.
  2. Pick a new workspace, then choose Merge and Rename conflicting tags, triggers and variables. GTM preselects Overwrite, which would replace your container, so change it.
  3. Check the preview shows 26 added, 0 modified and 0 deleted, then confirm.
  4. Set BC - GA4 Measurement ID to your ID.
  5. For Google Ads, set BC - Google Ads Conversion ID and BC - Google Ads Conversion Label, then unpause GAds - BC purchase (paused). It imports paused so it can't fire with placeholders. If you already have a purchase tag, delete this one and point yours at the new variables.
  6. Set testCoupons in the tracker tag, then go straight to Step 8.
What I checked: GTM's import screen accepted this file and showed that preview. I didn't complete an import into the live store, because its container already had the same setup built by hand. Check it in Preview, as in Step 9.

Or build it by hand

This is how I built it the first time, and it's worth doing if you want to know what each piece does.

  1. In GTM, go to Tags > New > Custom HTML.
  2. Paste the whole of gtm-paste.html.
  3. Edit the config block at the top if you need to (options below).
  4. Set the trigger to All Pages and save. Don't publish yet.
[[img:gtm-tracker-tag|The tag, its config block and the All Pages trigger.]]
window.BC_ECOM_CONFIG = {
  debug: false,          // true logs every push to the console
  userData: 'plain',     // 'plain' | 'hashed' | 'off'
  purchaseValue: 'net',  // 'net' | 'total'
  testCoupons: []        // e.g. ['MYTEST']
};
OptionWhat it does
userDataplain puts normalized customer data on the purchase push. hashed uses SHA-256 values. off sends none
purchaseValuenet follows Google's spec. total sends the full order total
testCouponsOrders with these codes push purchase_test, with no customer data
Set testCoupons. Excluding test orders in GA4 doesn't stop your Google Ads purchase tag from firing, so this is what keeps QA out of your conversions. Treat the code as private: a 100% coupon is a free order, so don't leave it in a screenshot or a public file.

Optional: the order ID helper

In GTM, the script reads the order number from the confirmation page. That worked in testing, but it isn't a documented BigCommerce feature. As a backup, add this in Script Manager with Placement Footer, Location Order confirmation and Script type Script:

<script>window.bcOrderId = '{{checkout.order.id}}';</script>
Step 4: Create the ecommerce trigger

The tag now pushes events, but nothing in GTM is listening for them yet. That's the trigger's job.

Go to Triggers > New > Custom Event, tick Use regex matching, and use this event name:

^(view_item_list|select_item|view_item|add_to_cart|remove_from_cart|view_cart|begin_checkout|add_shipping_info|add_payment_info|purchase)$
[[img:gtm-ecommerce-trigger|The field scrolls sideways, so check the full regex after pasting.]]
Compare against your existing trigger. An older one might leave out view_item_list, as the store I worked on did. Without it, the event reaches the dataLayer but never reaches GA4. purchase_test is left out on purpose.
Step 5: Send the events to GA4

With the trigger in place, GA4 is the easy part. One tag handles everything.

  1. Create a Google Analytics: GA4 Event tag.
  2. Set your Measurement ID, and set Event Name to {{Event}}.
  3. Under More Settings > Ecommerce, tick Send Ecommerce data with the source set to Data Layer.
  4. Use the trigger from Step 4.
[[img:gtm-ga4-ecommerce-tag|One GA4 tag handles every ecommerce event.]]
Keep user_data out of GA4. Don't add it as an event parameter. GA4's terms prohibit personal data in event parameters.

Keyword searches arrive as search, which is deliberately not in the regex. If you already track site search, as many containers do with view_search_results, decide on one before adding the other.
Step 6: Set up enhanced conversions

This was the part I most wanted to clean up. The old setup relied on two scripts happening to merge in GTM. Now all the customer data sits in one push.

The script pushes user_data at the top level of the purchase event, not inside ecommerce. Create one Data Layer Variable (Version 2) for each field:

Data Layer Variable NameUser-Provided Data field
user_data.emailEmail
user_data.phone_numberPhone
user_data.address.first_nameFirst Name
user_data.address.last_nameLast Name
user_data.address.streetStreet
user_data.address.cityCity
user_data.address.regionRegion
user_data.address.countryCountry
user_data.address.postal_codePostal Code
[[img:gtm-user-data-email-variable|One variable per field, starting with the email.]]

Then create a User-Provided Data variable, choose Manual configuration, and map each field.

[[img:gtm-user-provided-data|All nine fields mapped in the User-Provided Data variable.]]
If you're migrating from the Affiliate Conversion Tracking script, your old variable probably reads ecommerce.purchase.actionField.enhanced_conversion_data.email. That path only worked because GTM merged two pushes. The new script clears ecommerce before each event, so the old path will come back empty. Change the variable in the same release.

Good to know about this data:

  • In plain mode, customer data is readable on the confirmation page by any script there, and GTM's copy is cleared after 5 seconds. Choose hashed if you'd rather not expose it.
  • Phone is only sent when the dial code is known: a number starting with +, or a US or Canadian billing address.
  • Customer data is left out when BODL reports advertising consent as refused.
  • The push also includes meta_user_data and event_id if you use the Meta Pixel.
Step 7: Update your Google Ads purchase tag

Next came the Google Ads tag. The change here looks small, but it can move your reported numbers, so read the note on value before you touch it.

Point your conversion tag at the new values and fire it on a Custom Event trigger for purchase:

FieldData Layer Variable
Conversion Valueecommerce.value
Transaction IDecommerce.transaction_id
Currency Codeecommerce.currency
Itemsecommerce.items
User-provided dataYour variable from Step 6
[[img:gtm-google-ads-purchase-tag|Conversion ID and label replaced with placeholders.]]
Your conversion value will probably drop. Google's event reference says value is the sum of price times quantity, without tax or shipping, and net follows that. If your old tag sent the order total, values fall on launch day. Tell whoever owns the account and review any value-based bidding targets first. To keep the order total, set purchaseValue: 'total'.

Either way, GA4 revenue won't always match BigCommerce. The purchase push includes order_total, so you can reconcile:

{
  event: "purchase",
  event_id: "purchase_1001",
  ecommerce: {
    transaction_id: "1001",
    currency: "USD",
    value: 9.99,          // items after discounts
    tax: 0.70,
    shipping: 6.80,       // shipping + handling
    order_total: 17.49,   // what the customer paid
    coupon: "SAVE10",
    items: [{ item_id: "SKU123", item_name: "Display cable", price: 9.99, quantity: 1 }]
  },
  user_data: {
    email: "jane@example.com",
    phone_number: "+18475550100",
    address: { first_name: "jane", last_name: "doe", street: "1 main st", city: "chicago", region: "il", postal_code: "60601", country: "US" }
  },
  meta_user_data: { em: "jane@example.com", ph: "18475550100" }
}

Coupons and order discounts are spread across the items, so price is the discounted unit price and discount shows the difference.
Step 8: Remove every old ecommerce script

Everything so far is still sitting safely in a GTM workspace. This step is different, because taking the old scripts away changes what's live. On my store that meant the one-per-event scripts and the Affiliate Conversion Tracking script.

Do this as close to publishing as you can. Old scripts and the new tag together double count. Check all of these:

  • Script Manager: Storefront > Script Manager, or Channel Manager > your storefront > Script manager on multi-storefront.
  • Data Solutions: Settings > Data solutions, including Affiliate Conversion Tracking and any Google Analytics connection.
  • Theme files: especially if a developer added tracking in the past.
Two things to watch for here:
1. A deleted script can linger. Mine had gone from home, cart and web pages but was still served on category, brand and product pages. It cleared after other script changes, and I can't say exactly what cleared it. BigCommerce documents a 20-second script cache, and I found no purge option in Settings.
2. New scripts can take time. A new script took about 5 minutes to appear on the store, so wait before deciding it failed.

If events still fire twice, press Ctrl+U on the affected page and search the source for the old script's comment or event names. When pausing the new tag leaves one push behind, something else is still pushing.
Step 9: Test in GTM Preview

Before publishing, I went through the store as a shopper in Preview, checking one event at a time.

  1. Click Preview and connect to your store.
  2. Open a category page. Expect one view_item_list.
  3. Open a product page. Expect one view_item with quantity 1.
  4. Add the product. Expect one add_to_cart at the pre-tax price.
  5. On the cart page, expect one view_cart. Raise and lower the quantity, wait about 2 seconds each time, and expect add_to_cart and remove_from_cart for just the difference. Then remove the item.
  6. Go through checkout. Expect one each of begin_checkout, add_shipping_info and add_payment_info.
  7. Place an order with your test coupon. Expect purchase_test, and no Google Ads purchase tag.
  8. Reload the confirmation page. Expect nothing new.
[[img:gtm-preview-add-to-cart|Click the event, then Data Layer, and check price, quantity and value.]]
Checkout quirks you may run into with a 100% coupon:
  • Applying it after choosing shipping can show "Your shipping price has been updated". Click OK, choose the shipping method again and continue.
  • After your first test order, checkout may offer a sign-in for that email. Click Continue as guest.
  • Label test orders clearly in the name, company and comments. BigCommerce may flag or cancel a $0 order, and whoever fulfils orders will see it.
A test coupon can't confirm your purchase tags. It pushes purchase_test by design. To check purchase and user_data, place one real low-value order and refund it. Also, add_payment_info fires when the buyer reaches the payment step, before entering a card, because that's when BODL sends it.
Step 10: Publish, then check what actually went live

Everything looked right in Preview, so the workspace went live. I could have stopped there, and I'm glad I didn't.

Submit the workspace, and then check the published container. This is the mistake I nearly missed. Preview tests your workspace, so everything can pass there while the live container is still on an older version. I found a live container that had the tracker but not the enhanced conversion changes.

Open this in your browser, with your own container ID:

https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js?id=GTM-XXXXXXX

Search the file for BC_ECOM_CONFIG and user_data.email. Both should be there, and enhanced_conversion_data should be gone. You can also check the script from the console on any store page:

window.__bcEcom.status()

Then send bc_ecom_error to GA4 and set an alert, so you find out when BigCommerce changes before your reports go quiet:

error_typeWhat it means
bodl_missingBODL never loaded. Check Step 1
bodl_events_changedA BODL method the script uses has gone
cart_api_failed, cart_shapeThe Cart API failed or looks different
order_id_missingNo order number on the confirmation page. Add the helper from Step 3
order_api_failed, order_shapeThe Orders API failed or looks different
hash_unavailablehashed mode without browser crypto
script_exceptionAn error inside the script. The store isn't affected

Finally, note the launch date. Expect a drop in purchase value, new item category values (Shop By Type/Monitors becomes item_category and item_category2), and possible double counting while old scripts cleared.
The last test: a real paid order

Everything so far had run on $0 test orders, and those can't settle the question that matters. A test coupon pushes purchase_test by design, so it says nothing about your real purchase event or the customer data behind it.

So the last test was a real paid order on the live store, placed after everything was published. It worked as expected, and that's when I called the job done. If you follow this guide, do the same: one low-value order, checked in Preview, and refunded afterwards. It's the only test that exercises the path your real customers take.

That was the GTM route, and it's the one I'd recommend. It won't suit every store, though, which is why the second route exists.
Installing through Script Manager instead

Use this if your container blocks Custom HTML, or you'd rather not use GTM for the script. Skip Step 3 and do this instead. Steps 4 to 10 are the same.

  1. Go to Script Manager > Create a script.
  2. Give it a name, without brackets or symbols. Script names can't include them.
  3. Keep Placement on Footer.
[[img:bc-script-manager-create|Name it first, then set the location below.]]
  1. Set Location to All pages. This is the option that includes checkout and order confirmation, and "Storefront pages" does not.
  2. Set Script type to Script, paste script-manager-paste.html, and save.
[[img:bc-script-manager-all-pages|All pages and Script type selected, before pasting the file.]]

This version gets the order number from BigCommerce through Handlebars, so it doesn't need the helper. It stayed empty on other pages in testing, as it should.

Script category. It decides when the script can load if the store uses the cookie consent banner. In my test, a script on Analytics hadn't appeared after a couple of minutes. After switching it to Essential and waiting about 5 minutes it had, but because new scripts are slow to appear anyway, I can't say the category was the cause. Choose what matches your consent policy, and check the page source.
Script Manager has no Preview. It's live for shoppers as soon as it appears. To test safely, set dataLayerName: 'testLayer' and userData: 'off' so your tags can't see the events, check window.testLayer in the console, and then remove those settings.

What I tested, and what I didn't

One store and one paid order is real evidence, but it isn't every store. I ran 27 automated tests, then tested on one live store: Stencil theme, tax-exclusive pricing, USD and guest shoppers. That covered the events above, button and link add to cart, quantity changes, removal, $0 test orders, reload protection and purchase_test. I also ran real installs of the hosted file through GTM Preview and temporarily through Script Manager, and the final check was a real paid order.

Not yet verified on a live store:

  • Logged-in customers, variants with options, sale prices, digital items, bundles and gift certificates
  • Tax-inclusive stores, where cart event values include tax because the Cart API prices do
  • Multi-currency stores, and order-level discounts other than coupons
  • Other themes

Other limits: refunds, phone orders and buyers who never reach the confirmation page aren't tracked. Reload protection uses localStorage, so the same order opened in another browser can fire again, and transaction_id is there to deduplicate it.
Frequently asked questions

Does BigCommerce have built-in GA4 ecommerce tracking?

Data Solutions has a native Google Analytics 4 connection. If you track through GTM, pick one route for GA4, because sending the same events both ways can double count.

Can I use GTM alone without Script Manager?

Yes, as long as GTM loads on checkout and order confirmation. The order ID helper in Script Manager is optional.

Should purchase value include tax and shipping?

Google's event reference says no, and that's the default here. Some teams prefer the order total for Google Ads, which is why purchaseValue: 'total' exists.

Why was my purchase event missing after I enabled a test coupon?

That's working as intended. Orders with a coupon in testCoupons push purchase_test, so they don't count as conversions.

Does it work on Catalyst or headless BigCommerce?

No. It's built for hosted Stencil storefronts.

Is the script free?

Yes, it's MIT licensed and on GitHub.

Is there a GTM import file?

Yes. It sets up the tracker, triggers, GA4 tags, enhanced conversions variables and a paused Google Ads tag. See Step 3.
closing: If you'd rather have this installed and checked for you, or your numbers still don't add up after following this guide, I can help.
